Open knowledge as an act of care

I learned to code from strangers on the internet.

Not from a bootcamp (I couldn't afford one at the time). Not from a university curriculum. From Stack Overflow answers written at midnight, from documentation someone decided to translate into Portuguese, from a GitHub repository someone open-sourced on a Tuesday afternoon for no particular reason.

Those strangers didn't know I existed. They couldn't have known that a teenager in Brazil would stumble across what they'd written and use it to change the direction of her life. But they wrote it anyway. They published it openly. They left the light on.

I think about that a lot.

Knowledge hoarding is a power structure

There's a version of expertise that is built on scarcity. The consultant who never fully explains their process. The senior developer who answers questions vaguely so that juniors stay dependent. The platform that walls off documentation behind a premium tier.

These aren't neutral choices. They're decisions about who gets to participate, who gets to build, who gets to grow.

Open knowledge is a counter-proposal. It says: what I know is more valuable shared than hoarded. It says: my expertise isn't diminished by your understanding of it. It says: the commons matter.

What open source actually taught me

The code is almost secondary.

What open source taught me:

  • How to receive feedback in public. Your PR gets comments. Sometimes harsh ones. You learn to separate your ego from your output. This is an extremely useful skill in every area of life.

  • How to write for strangers. A good README is an act of radical hospitality. You're writing for someone you've never met, in a context you can't predict, with a patience you have to manufacture.

  • That maintenance is care. The romantic image of open source is the initial contribution, the clever solution, the commit that changes everything. The unglamorous reality is: responding to issues at 11pm, writing changelogs, bumping dependencies. This is what keeping a project alive actually looks like. It looks like care.

What I want to do with this

I'm not a famous developer. I don't have a library with ten thousand GitHub stars. But I can:

  • Write down what I learn, openly, in public
  • Contribute to projects I use, even if my contribution is fixing a typo in the docs
  • Answer questions in communities where people are learning
  • Build things that are themselves open — this blog is a start

None of this is heroic. It's just leaving the light on.

For whoever needs it next.
